_comment: Short, one-paragraph introductions shown at the top of each book page. Keyed by the page slug rather than the book's name: book_blurbs.json derives its key by slugifying the name it carries, which silently lost Al-Tawḥīd and Muʿjam al-Aḥādīth al-Muʿtabara when that name did not match the catalogue's. These are deliberately brief - a reader who wants the long form has the collection itself.
al-kafi: Compiled by Muḥammad b. Yaʿqūb al-Kulaynī (d. 329/941) over some twenty years, al-Kāfi is the earliest and most widely cited of the Four Books. It is arranged in three parts: the Uṣūl on belief, the Furūʿ on law and practice, and the Rawḍa, a miscellany of letters and sermons.
man-la-yahduruh-al-faqih: The second of the Four Books, written by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (d. 381/991) as a working reference rather than an archive. Its title - 'for one who has no jurist at hand' - is its method: narrations the author considered reliable enough to act upon, arranged for someone who must decide a question alone.
nahj-al-balagha: Sermons, letters and short sayings of Imam ʿAlī, selected by al-Sharīf al-Raḍī (d. 406/1015). Gathered for their eloquence as much as their content, it has been read as a masterwork of Arabic prose and as a source on governance, justice and the nature of the world.
al-amali: The 'dictations' of Shaykh al-Ṣadūq: narrations recorded as he delivered them in teaching sessions, each assembly dated. The result reads less like a compiled reference than a record of what was actually being taught, and to whom.
al-khisal: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq's collection arranged by number: traditions that enumerate one thing, then two, then three, and onward. The ordering is a mnemonic device rather than a subject index, which makes it a book of lists on everything from ethics to cosmology.
kitab-al-ghayba: Shaykh al-Ṭūsī's (d. 460/1067) treatment of the occultation of the twelfth Imam - the reports concerning it, the arguments for it, and the objections raised against it. It is the principal early Imāmī work on the subject.
thawab-al-a-mal-wa-iqab-al-a-mal: Paired collections by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq on the rewards promised for particular deeds and the punishments warned of for particular sins. Read together, they are a map of what the tradition treats as consequential.
uyun-akhbar-al-rida: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq's gathering of reports concerning ʿAlī b. Mūsā al-Riḍā, the eighth Imam - his sayings, his correspondence, and accounts of his life, including his years in Khurāsān and the debates he is recorded as holding there.
ma-ani-al-akhbar: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq on the meanings of the reports: narrations gathered specifically to explain difficult words and obscure phrases found elsewhere in hadith. It is a commentary assembled entirely out of other narrations.
kamil-al-ziyarat: Ibn Qūlawayh's (d. 368/978) collection on ziyāra - the visitation of the Prophet and the Imams, and above all of Imam al-Ḥusayn at Karbalā. It is cited as much for its author's statement about the sources he drew on as for its contents.
al-tawhid: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq on divine unity: narrations on God's attributes, His names, and the rejection of any likeness between God and created things. It was written against anthropomorphism, and its arrangement follows that argument.
mu-jam-al-ahadith-al-mu-tabara: A modern compilation restricted to narrations its compiler judged reliable by explicit criteria. Where the classical collections gather and leave assessment to the reader, this one applies the assessment first, which makes it useful for seeing which reports survive a strict standard.
kitab-al-zuhd: An early collection by al-Ḥusayn b. Saʿīd al-Ahwāzī on renunciation - detachment from the world, restraint, and the fear and hope that the tradition treats as the proper posture toward it. Its author belongs to the generation whose books the later compilers drew upon.
kitab-al-du-afa: Not a hadith collection but a work of rijāl: entries on narrators its author, Ibn al-Ghaḍāʾirī, judged weak or unreliable. It is consulted when weighing a chain of transmission, and its severity is itself a subject of scholarly argument.
kitab-al-mu-min: Al-Ḥusayn b. Saʿīd al-Ahwāzī on the believer: the standing of a believer before God, the rights believers hold over one another, and the weight the tradition places on how they are treated.
sifat-al-shi-a: A short collection by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq describing what the Shīʿa are held to be - the conduct, obligations and character the narrations attach to the name, stated as a standard rather than a description.
risalat-al-huquq: The Treatise on Rights, attributed to Imam Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn: a single sustained enumeration of the rights owed - to God, to one's own limbs and faculties, to those one leads, follows, teaches, is taught by, and lives among. It is unusual in the corpus for being one continuous argument rather than a gathering of reports.
fada-il-al-shi-a: A brief collection by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq on the merits promised to the Shīʿa. It is a companion to Ṣifāt al-Shīʿa, and the two are usually read together.
